text: IAM users and groups cover identities inside your own account, but AWS applications and services often need access too, without a person ever sitting at a keyboard. That's what IAM roles solve, and this lesson covers what a role actually is, how it issues temporary credentials, and why it beats a long-lived access key for anything running on AWS infrastructure.

A role looks like an IAM user in one way — permission policies get attached to it — but it has no password and no permanent access keys of its own. Instead, a role is assumed: a trusted entity, which could be a user, an application, or an AWS service like EC2, temporarily takes on its permissions and then the credentials expire automatically. Every role carries a trust policy, a document that says exactly who or what is allowed to assume it in the first place.

This trust policy allows only the EC2 service itself to assume the role — nothing else is permitted to. When EC2 assumes it, AWS's Security Token Service issues a temporary access key, secret key, and session token, valid for a limited window, and those credentials simply stop working once that window ends. No manual cleanup, no rotation schedule to remember.

Here's where that matters in practice. An application on an EC2 instance needs to read files from S3. The risky shortcut is generating an IAM user's access key and pasting it into a config file on the instance, where it can leak from a repo, a log, or a stolen laptop. The real-practice alternative attaches a role, with S3 read permissions, to the instance as an instance profile. The application calls S3 using temporary credentials AWS manages automatically — no long-lived key was ever created, so there was never anything to leak.

That's why AWS guidance consistently recommends roles over user access keys for anything running on AWS infrastructure: nothing static to rotate, nothing to accidentally commit to a repository. Next, Lesson 4 moves up a level, to AWS Organizations and managing many accounts — not just many identities — from one place.
